core: The Cold War as the roughly 1947-1991 geopolitical and ideological rivalry between the U.S.-led West and the USSR-led East
The ideological clash: democratic capitalism vs. Soviet communism, and how WWII allies became rivals after 1945
The division of Europe: the 'iron curtain' (Churchill, Fulton, March 5, 1946), a divided Germany and Berlin
U.S. containment policy: George Kennan's Long Telegram, the Truman Doctrine (March 12, 1947), the Marshall Plan (1947)
Why it was 'cold' — no direct U.S.-USSR war — alongside a nuclear arms race and mutually assured destruction (MAD)
The Berlin Blockade and Airlift (June 1948-May 12, 1949); NATO (1949) and the Warsaw Pact (1955)
The space race (Sputnik October 4, 1957; Gagarin 1961; Apollo 11 July 1969)
Hot proxy wars: Korea (June 25, 1950-July 27, 1953) and Vietnam; the Berlin Wall (built August 1961)
The Cuban Missile Crisis (October 1962) as the closest brush with nuclear war
The end: Gorbachev's reforms (glasnost and perestroika, from 1985), the fall of the Berlin Wall (November 9, 1989), and the dissolution of the Soviet Union (December 1991)
supporting: Détente as a phase of eased tension in the 1970s
Even-handed treatment: both superpowers armed heavily and intervened abroad
Multiple/contingent causation and distinguishing fact from interpretation

The full history of decolonization and imperialism (named as intertwined, not owned)

claims.claim: The Cold War was a roughly 1947-1991 geopolitical and ideological rivalry between the United States and its allies (democratic capitalism) and the Soviet Union and its allies (communism); after Germany's surrender in May 1945 the wartime 'Big Three' allies quickly divided over incompatible postwar goals.

On March 5, 1946, in a speech at Fulton, Missouri ('The Sinews of Peace'), Winston Churchill declared that an 'iron curtain' had descended across Europe, dividing a Soviet-dominated East from the West.

U.S. strategy centered on containment—confining Soviet influence rather than rolling it back—first framed by diplomat George Kennan in his 1946 'Long Telegram'; it was implemented through the Truman Doctrine (announced March 12, 1947, aiding Greece and Turkey) and the Marshall Plan (proposed 1947), which sent roughly $12-13 billion to rebuild Western Europe.

Germany and its capital Berlin (inside the Soviet zone) were divided into Western and Soviet sectors; after a new Western currency was introduced, the USSR blockaded land routes into West Berlin in June 1948, and the Western allies supplied the city by the Berlin Airlift until the Soviets lifted the blockade on May 12, 1949.

Rival alliances formed: NATO (North Atlantic Treaty Organization) in 1949 among Western states, and the Warsaw Pact in 1955 among the USSR and its Eastern European allies after West Germany joined NATO.

The war stayed 'cold' because the U.S. and USSR never fought each other directly; caution was enforced by a nuclear arms race (Soviet atomic bomb 1949, U.S. hydrogen bomb 1952, ICBMs in the 1950s) and the doctrine of mutually assured destruction (MAD).

The space race was a Cold War competition: the Soviet Union launched the first satellite, Sputnik, on October 4, 1957, and put the first human (Yuri Gagarin) into orbit in 1961; the United States landed astronauts on the Moon (Apollo 11) in July 1969.

The superpowers fought through proxy wars: the Korean War (June 25, 1950-armistice July 27, 1953), which killed roughly three million people (mostly civilians), and the Vietnam War (Second Indochina War, from 1959).
The East German government built the Berlin Wall in August 1961 to stop citizens fleeing to the West.

The Cuban Missile Crisis of October 1962—triggered when U.S. reconnaissance discovered Soviet nuclear missile sites under construction in Cuba on October 14—brought the superpowers closest to nuclear war; after about thirteen days, Khrushchev agreed on October 28 to withdraw the missiles in exchange for a U.S. pledge not to invade Cuba, with U.S. Jupiter missiles quietly removed from Turkey by April 1963.

The Cold War ended without a direct war: Mikhail Gorbachev (in power from 1985) introduced glasnost ('openness') and perestroika ('restructuring'), cut military spending, and eased the Soviet grip on Eastern Europe; largely peaceful revolutions swept Eastern Europe in 1989, the Berlin Wall fell on November 9, 1989, Germany reunified in 1990, and the Soviet Union dissolved in December 1991.

Assessed even-handedly, both superpowers built vast nuclear arsenals and intervened in other nations to advance their own security and ideology; the Cold War is best analyzed as a rivalry of two superpowers rather than a simple good-versus-evil story.

conflictingEvidence.issue: The exact start and end dates of the Cold War
positions: Some date the start to 1945 (end of WWII / Big Three split), others to 1947 (Truman Doctrine / containment) or Churchill's 1946 Iron Curtain speech
The end is variously dated to the fall of the Berlin Wall (1989) or the dissolution of the USSR (1991)
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson uses the widely taught 'roughly 1947-1991' framing while naming the 1945 divergence and the 1946 Iron Curtain speech as origins and treating 1989-1991 as the end, noting these are conventional markers rather than precise boundaries.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Interpreting responsibility for the Cold War
positions: A traditional Western view emphasizes Soviet expansionism as the driver
Revisionist and post-revisionist scholarship stresses mutual misperception, both sides' security fears, and shared responsibility
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson states facts (who did what, when) even-handedly and frames causation as a clash of ideology and security on both sides, without declaring one superpower solely responsible.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft was generic boilerplate ('Cold War is a foundational concept in History...') with no substantive historical claims, dates, or sources; nothing in it could be verified or reused.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced the entire boilerplate draft with researched, date-verified content.

Fixed a date hazard flagged during research: an automated extraction rendered Churchill's Iron Curtain speech as 'March 12, 1946' (a confusion with the March 12, 1947 Truman Doctrine); the verified date is March 5, 1946, confirmed via the National WWII Museum and corroborating sources.
Stated proxy-war human costs plainly (Korea ~3 million dead, mostly civilians) to avoid the common misconception that a 'cold' war meant no casualties.
Adopted deliberately even-handed framing per the source-map control: both superpowers armed heavily and intervened abroad; avoided triumphalist 'the West won' language.

sourceRecords.notes: Supports the ideological clash (democratic capitalism vs. communism), the post-1945 split of the wartime allies, Churchill's Iron Curtain image (Fulton, March 1946), containment and George Kennan's Long Telegram, the Truman Doctrine (March 12, 1947) and Marshall Plan (~$12-13 billion), the division of Germany/Berlin, the Berlin Blockade (June 1948) and Airlift ending May 1949, NATO (1949) and the Warsaw Pact (1955), and the nuclear arms race and MAD. CC BY 4.0, but used reference-only; prose is original. Read directly via WebFetch.

sourceRecords.notes: Supports the proxy-war dimension: the Korean War (invasion June 25, 1950; armistice July 27, 1953) with roughly three million deaths, most of them Korean civilians; the beginning of the Vietnam War (Second Indochina War) in 1959; and the establishment of the People's Republic of China (October 1, 1949). CC BY 4.0, used reference-only. Read directly via WebFetch.

sourceRecords.title: World History, Volume 2, 14.5 A New World Order
sourceRecords.notes: Supports the end of the Cold War: Gorbachev's rise (1985) and his reforms glasnost ('openness') and perestroika ('restructuring'), cuts to military spending, the 1989 opening of borders and the tearing down of the Berlin Wall, German reunification (1990), the failed August 1991 hard-line coup, and the December 1991 dissolution of the Soviet Union. Also corroborates the Berlin Wall's construction context. CC BY 4.0, used reference-only. Read directly via WebFetch.

sourceRecords.notes: Corroborates (U.S. perspective) containment and the Truman Doctrine, the Berlin Blockade (Stalin cut land and water routes into West Berlin in June 1948) and its end on May 12, 1949 after roughly two million tons of airlifted supplies, and the Korean War (North Korean crossing of the 38th parallel June 25, 1950; armistice July 27, 1953). CC BY 4.0, used reference-only. Read directly via WebFetch.

sourceRecords.notes: Authoritative U.S. government (public domain) source for the Cuban Missile Crisis: Khrushchev's July 1962 agreement with Castro to place missiles in Cuba; the October 14, 1962 U-2 discovery of missile sites; Kennedy's naval 'quarantine' announced October 22; the roughly 13-day confrontation; Khrushchev's October 28 agreement to withdraw the missiles in exchange for a U.S. no-invasion pledge; and the removal of U.S. Jupiter missiles from Turkey in April 1963. sourceRecords.title: Winston Churchill's Iron Curtain Speech-March 5, 1946
sourceRecords.notes: Confirms the exact date and setting of Churchill's 'Sinews of Peace' (Iron Curtain) speech: March 5, 1946, at Westminster College, Fulton, Missouri, with President Truman present. Used to correct an automated extraction that had rendered the date as March 12, 1946. Corroborated by Britannica and the National Churchill Museum via search. Read via search result summary of the museum article.

sourceRecords.title: 65 Years Ago: Sputnik Ushers in the Space Age
sourceRecords.notes: Authoritative NASA (public domain) source confirming the Soviet launch of Sputnik 1 on October 4, 1957, as the start of the space age and the U.S.-Soviet space race, which spurred the U.S. response leading to the creation of NASA in 1958. The dates for Gagarin (April 12, 1961) and Apollo 11 (July 20, 1969) are additionally corroborated by Britannica and multiple sources. Read via search result summary of the NASA article.
